title: Field Shift — Story County, Iowa
disclaimer: This tool is meant to support, not replace, farmer judgment and local agricultural expertise. Indicators use NASA and public soils/crop data with documented approximations (FAO-56 crop coefficients, cover-crop bare-month assumptions). Yields, markets, leases, and equipment are not modelled.

metrics.caveat: One seed (42), not a published benchmark. Trained on a random sample of farmed 30 m pixels in Story County, Iowa. Temporal split: train 2014-2021 (after 5-year lags from 2009), validation 2022-2023, test 2024-2025.

calibration.method: temperature scaling fit on validation years 2022-2023

featured.reason: Steepest analysis tile — erosion trade-offs are most visible here.
Lowest next-season model confidence — an 'ask your agronomist' case.
Tile with more hay or grass in the recent CDL record.

strategies.name: Current corn-soy
strategies.why: The dominant Story County rotation in the CDL record. Baseline that most fields already follow.
strategies.benefits: Familiar markets, existing equipment, well-understood agronomy.
strategies.risks: Long bare windows after harvest raise erosion risk on sloped ground. Continuous row crops add little nitrogen and can tighten pest cycles.
strategies.gaps: Does not include a winter cover or a small-grain/hay break. Local yield and lease constraints are not modelled.

strategies.name: Diversified small-grain / hay
strategies.why: Inserts a small-grain year and a hay year into the corn-soy cycle to break pest cycles and keep a living root in the ground longer.
strategies.benefits: Higher nitrogen-fixing share (soy + hay), fewer bare months, added forage option.
strategies.risks: Hay and small-grain markets and equipment needs differ from a pure corn-soy operation. Forage value is farm-specific.
strategies.gaps: other_crop is a CDL residual class (oats, wheat, vegetables, etc.), not a single recommended cultivar.

strategies.name: Cover-crop conservation
strategies.why: Keeps the current cash-crop rotation but adds a winter rye cover to shrink bare-soil months and cut erosion, especially on steeper tiles.
strategies.benefits: Lower erosion risk and slightly better infiltration; modest winter water use.
strategies.risks: Cover termination timing, herbicide program, and spring soil moisture can affect the following cash crop. Not a yield model.
strategies.gaps: Cover crops are not visible as a main-season CDL class; bare-month reduction is a documented assumption, not a satellite detection of rye on these fields.

pareto.note: NSGA-II (48 individuals, 25 generations, seed 42) over 4-year sequences drawn from corn, soy, hay, grass, other_crop, and a winter-rye cover variant. One seed, not a published benchmark.

help.water_demand: Relative mid-season crop coefficient (FAO-56 style) averaged over the 4-year sequence. Lower is less water demand. Not a field-calibrated ET estimate.
help.erosion_risk: NASADEM slope combined with typical bare-soil months (shrunk when a winter cover is included, or when the crop is hay/grass). Lower is better.
help.n_fixing_share: Share of years in soy (full) or hay (partial, alfalfa/mixed hay). Higher can support nitrogen supply; it is not a fertilizer recommendation.
help.heat_frost_exposure: Blend of growing-degree-day shortfall vs crop need, spring frost days, and days ≥ 32 °C from NASA POWER. Lower is better.
help.soil_moisture_stress: How sensitive the crop is to low NASA POWER root-zone wetness (GWETROOT). Lower is better. SMAP is not included (needs Earthdata login).
